Q3 option 1 is a distractor; Sèvres did assign some Anatolian/Aegean territory to Greece and Italy, but not Arab lands, so it's cleanly wrong. Q4 option 3 (Quit India, 1942) is clearly a distractor. Everything checks out.

Audit: Q1 stem says "main claim... affected the people who made goods" — Wells says craftsmen either became employers or sank to labourers; option 3 says "a few rising employers and many unskilled laborers." Wells doesn't quantify "few/many," but it's a reasonable gloss; minor. Q5 is sound. Q3 is contextual (not in excerpt) but accurate. No real problems.

Audit: Q5 option [3] is the 1949 Chinese Civil War victory, which falls outside the "1950 to 1975" window stated in the stem and is a consequence that would run counter to the policy anyway—a distractor, fine. Q5 option [1] Bandung: Truman Doctrine arguably contributed indirectly to bipolar pressure that non-alignment reacted against, but "most directly" clearly favors Korea/Vietnam. Q3: the Greek civil war was primarily between the Greek government and communist insurgents backed by Yugoslavia/Albania/Bulgaria more than the USSR directly, but the option's phrasing ("Soviet pressure on Turkey") is accurate; Britain's withdrawal of aid notice in February 1947 is correct. Q4 stem relies on the context line (Congress) appropriately. No real issues.

Audit notes: Q4's stem says the Battle of Panipat is "described in the context line" — accurate. Q5 options are factually wrong distractors by design (Persian composition, Akbar-era writing) — not flagged. Q6's "largely Hindu population" is accurate for northern India in the 1520s. Q1 option 0 is a reasonable inference; "farmers" isn't in the excerpt but the question says "help explain," so acceptable. No real problems found.

Audit: The stimulus is accurately quoted and described. Q1 distractors are anachronistic as causes (WTO 2001, USSR collapse 1991, IMF conditionality never applied to China), which is appropriate for distractors. Q2 option 0 accurately paraphrases "benefited the Chinese economy but also integrated China into the world economy." Q3 option 1 is the only direct evidence of integration. Q4 option 2 correctly situates reform in the late-20th-century neoliberal/market turn. Q5 option 3 is the only post-1987 subject. Q6: Doi Moi (1986) is the clear parallel; the other options describe nationalization or autarky. No real problems found.

Audit notes: Q1 option 0 correctly describes a most-favored-nation clause; it is "one-sided" in the Kanagawa text (no reciprocal grant from the US). Q2 option 0's reference to seventeenth-century Tokugawa bans is accurate. Q5's stem says "along with later treaties of the same kind," which fairly links to the Harris Treaty and sonnō jōi agitation. Q6 option 1 states that the treaty omits the naval pressure, which matches the text and the context line. No real problems found.

Audit: The context line and image description accurately reflect the cartoon (Victoria, Wilhelm II, Nicholas II, Marianne, Japan, and a Qing official; Kiao-Tchéou and Port-Arthur labels). Stems are neutral and don't overreach the credit line. Q4 "within the next few years" fits the Boxer Rebellion (1899–1901), and the Shandong/Kiaochow connection is well established. Q5's Sino-Japanese War is the standard explanation for Japan's seat at the table. No real problems found.

Audit notes: Q6 option [1] says the cartoon "shows the railway as completed" — the cartoon shows a telegraph wire, not a railway; it is a distractor and wrong for a factual reason that is in-image, so not flagging as misdescription of the keyed answer.
